exhibits.title: The Telephone
exhibits.change: The human voice carried over a wire.
exhibits.context: Alexander Graham Bell's patent and first intelligible transmission came in 1876. Elisha Gray filed a caveat the same day and Antonio Meucci had earlier devices, so priority is contested. Exchanges and networks spread rapidly in cities.
exhibits.significance: Real-time conversation at a distance — the network later used by early computer links.

uncertainty.note: Priority between Bell, Gray and Meucci remains disputed.

exhibits.title: The Internal Combustion Engine
exhibits.change: Fuel burned inside the cylinder: compact, light power.
exhibits.context: Nicolaus Otto's four-stroke engine, following Lenoir's earlier gas engine, became the basis of petrol engines; Rudolf Diesel's compression-ignition engine followed in the 1890s.
exhibits.significance: Power small enough for cars, tractors, aircraft and generators.

exhibits.title: Recorded Sound
exhibits.change: A voice captured on tinfoil and played back.
exhibits.context: Thomas Edison's phonograph could record and replay sound. Édouard-Léon Scott's phonautograph (1857) had recorded sound waves but could not play them back.
exhibits.significance: Music and speech preserved beyond the moment.

exhibits.title: Electric Light
exhibits.change: A glowing filament in a vacuum: safe light at the flick of a switch.
exhibits.context: Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison developed practical incandescent lamps independently; they later merged their British interests. Arc lamps had lit streets earlier but were too harsh for homes.
exhibits.significance: Night became usable time — and the demand that drove electrical grids.

exhibits.title: Electrification

when.display: from 1882 (first central power stations); AC grids from the 1890s

exhibits.change: Power generated in one place and delivered to thousands of homes and factories by wire.
exhibits.context: Central generating stations opened in London and New York in 1882. Transformers and alternating current (Gaulard and Gibbs; Ganz; Tesla and Westinghouse) allowed long-distance transmission; the Niagara Falls hydroelectric plant (1895) supplied distant cities. Electrification spread over decades and is still incomplete for hundreds of millions of people.
exhibits.significance: Electric motors transformed factories, homes, cities and communication — the platform on which every later technology in this Museum runs.

exhibits.title: The Steel-Frame Skyscraper
exhibits.change: Walls hung on a metal skeleton — buildings could rise without thick walls.
exhibits.context: The Home Insurance Building in Chicago is often cited as the first skyscraper. Safety elevators (Otis, 1850s) made tall buildings usable.
exhibits.significance: The vertical city — density without thick walls.

exhibits.title: The Automobile
exhibits.change: A self-propelled road vehicle with a petrol engine.
exhibits.context: Carl Benz patented his Motorwagen in 1886; Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built a motorised carriage the same year. Bertha Benz's 1888 long-distance drive demonstrated its practicality.
exhibits.significance: Reshaped cities, landscapes, economies and the atmosphere.

exhibits.title: Radio
exhibits.change: Messages carried through the air, without wires.
exhibits.context: After Hertz generated electromagnetic waves, Guglielmo Marconi built practical wireless telegraphy; Jagadish Chandra Bose demonstrated microwave signalling and Popov a lightning detector and receiver. Marconi's signal crossed the Atlantic in 1901.
exhibits.significance: Wireless communication — broadcasting, radar, satellites and mobile phones descend from it.

uncertainty.note: Credit for inventing radio is shared and disputed.

exhibits.title: X-Rays
exhibits.change: Invisible rays showed the bones inside a living hand.
exhibits.context: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays while experimenting with cathode-ray tubes; within months they were used in medicine. Their dangers were learned painfully.
exhibits.significance: Seeing inside the body without surgery; later, the structure of crystals and DNA.

exhibits.title: Cinema
exhibits.change: Moving pictures projected for an audience.
exhibits.context: The Lumière brothers' Cinématographe screened films to a paying public in December 1895. Edison's Kinetoscope showed films to one viewer at a time.
exhibits.significance: A new art form and mass medium — the ancestor of television and video.

exhibits.title: Radioactivity
exhibits.change: Atoms were not eternal: some broke apart, releasing energy.
exhibits.context: Henri Becquerel found uranium emitted radiation; Marie and Pierre Curie discovered polonium and radium. Marie Curie became the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences.
exhibits.significance: Opened nuclear physics, radiometric dating (the clocks behind this Museum's early galleries) and radiation medicine.

exhibits.title: The Electron
exhibits.change: The first subatomic particle.
exhibits.context: J. J. Thomson showed cathode rays were streams of tiny charged particles far lighter than atoms.
exhibits.significance: Electronics — valves, transistors, chips — is the control of electrons.

exhibits.title: The Quantum
exhibits.change: Energy comes in discrete packets.
exhibits.context: Max Planck introduced energy quanta to explain black-body radiation; Albert Einstein explained the photoelectric effect with light quanta in 1905.
exhibits.significance: The beginning of quantum physics — the science behind lasers, semiconductors and chemistry itself.

exhibits.title: Blood Groups
exhibits.change: Why some transfusions killed and others saved lives.
exhibits.context: Karl Landsteiner identified the ABO blood groups, making safe transfusion possible; blood banks followed in the 1930s.
exhibits.significance: The basis of transfusion medicine and much of modern surgery.

exhibits.title: Powered Flight

site.label: Kill Devil Hills, Kitty Hawk, North Carolina

exhibits.change: A controllable, heavier-than-air machine flew under its own power.
exhibits.context: Orville and Wilbur Wright's Flyer made four flights on 17 December 1903, the longest 59 seconds. Their key insight was three-axis control, developed with glider tests and their own wind tunnel, building on Otto Lilienthal's gliding experiments. Within twelve years aircraft were being mass-produced for war.
exhibits.significance: The sky became a route. Within a lifetime people crossed oceans in hours — and, 66 years after Kitty Hawk, walked on the Moon.

exhibits.title: The Rocket Equation
exhibits.change: The mathematics of reaching space with rockets.
exhibits.context: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, a schoolteacher, published the relation between a rocket's speed, exhaust velocity and mass ratio, and proposed multi-stage rockets and liquid fuels.
exhibits.significance: The theoretical foundation of spaceflight.

exhibits.title: The Vacuum Tube
exhibits.change: A glass valve controlled and amplified electric signals.
exhibits.context: John Ambrose Fleming's diode rectified radio signals; Lee de Forest's triode amplified them, enabling radio broadcasting, long-distance telephony and, later, the first electronic computers.
exhibits.significance: The first active electronic component — electronics began here.

exhibits.title: Relativity
exhibits.change: Space and time are one fabric, bent by mass.
exhibits.context: Albert Einstein's special relativity (1905) linked mass and energy (E = mc²); general relativity (1915) explained gravity as curved spacetime, confirmed by the 1919 eclipse observations.
exhibits.significance: Needed for GPS, cosmology, black holes and gravitational waves.

exhibits.title: The First Synthetic Plastic
exhibits.change: A fully synthetic material moulded into any shape.
exhibits.context: Leo Baekeland's Bakelite, made from phenol and formaldehyde, was a heat-resistant insulator ideal for the electrical age. Semi-synthetic plastics such as celluloid came earlier.
exhibits.significance: The first of the plastics that now shape — and pollute — the modern world.

exhibits.title: Fertiliser from the Air
exhibits.change: Nitrogen pulled from the air and turned into ammonia.
exhibits.context: Fritz Haber's laboratory synthesis and Carl Bosch's high-pressure industrial process made synthetic nitrogen fertiliser — and explosives — on a vast scale.
exhibits.significance: Roughly half the world's population is fed by food grown with synthetic nitrogen; the process also has large environmental costs.

exhibits.title: The Moving Assembly Line
exhibits.change: The work moved past the workers — a car every few minutes.
exhibits.context: Ford's Highland Park plant cut assembly time for a Model T from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes, using interchangeable parts and electric-powered conveyors.
exhibits.significance: Mass production and mass consumption — and repetitive industrial labour.

exhibits.title: The Panama Canal
exhibits.change: Locks lifted ships across a continent between two oceans.
exhibits.context: After a failed French attempt in which tens of thousands died of disease and accidents, the US completed the canal, aided by mosquito control based on new understanding of yellow fever and malaria.
exhibits.significance: Engineering and public health combined to reshape world shipping.
